prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators, and the first experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall state in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: I move from magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene to topological insulators as my preferred single-part prize. The reasons are scientific. The Kane-Mele Z2 invariant is a bulk property that forces protected boundary states, and it was tested cleanly by Molenkamp's HgTe edge-channel transport in 2007. Since then it has been confirmed by transport, ARPES and STM in many independent laboratories, and first-principles calculations in my own field have predicted and then verified many topological materials. That is a stable interpretation after fifteen years or more, which is the robustness I asked of other candidates in round 1 and which magic-angle graphene cannot yet show. Four colleagues (Johansson, Mehlig, Olsson, Pearce) argued that the pairing mechanism, twist-angle disorder and an eight-year record make B013 premature, and I think they are right to weigh that. The chair's question about robustness across laboratories despite disorder does not have a decisive answer yet: the phenomena are reproduced, but the sample dependence is large and the pairing mechanism is open. B024 also has the broadest support and the clearest before-and-after structure, with the theory pair and the decisive experiment. I would keep the citation to the quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators and state explicitly that it concerns materials with protected boundary states, which separates it from the 2016 prize on topological phase transitions and quantised Hall conductance.
statement.case_against: Attribution is the real cost, and I do not want to hide it. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed HgTe quantum wells, which Molenkamp's group then tested, and Zhang is deceased. Fu, Kane and Moore, and Balents, extended the idea to three dimensions, and Hasan's ARPES observation of the 3D topological insulator is left unrecognised by this trio. The 2016 prize on topological phases will lead some to see this as a second helping of the same theme, and the practical consequences are still modest. If the committee judged that no three-name slate is defensible, I would fall back on B013, which has a cleaner theory-plus-experiment credit but is younger, or on B001, which has the cleanest names but whose distinctness I cannot judge.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers Kane, Mele and Molenkamp over a slate with Hasan, because the quantum spin Hall effect has a clean before and after, Hasan's 3D ARPES work is a follow-on, and omitting Mele, who shared the Z2 invariant from the start, is harder to defend than omitting the 3D step.
responses.response: I find this persuasive and I adopt that trio. Kane and Mele wrote the founding papers and the Z2 invariant is a joint result, so a prize on the theory should not split them. The 2007 HgTe experiment is the unambiguous experimental discovery. From the materials side, Hasan's ARPES work is important and I would like the citation not to deny it, but it generalises an idea already established, and my own area cannot make it a separate discovery. I accept that the cost is real, and I am not claiming the omission of Hasan or of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang is costless.

responses.point: Johansson prefers Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan so that the 3D topological insulator observation is not left unrecognised, and says that if no defensible trio exists the B024 case weakens. He also said he would move B013 up if the correlated phases were shown to be robust across laboratories despite disorder.
responses.response: I cannot give you that evidence in a form that would change the maturity assessment, and I would rather concede than argue it. The phenomena are reproduced, but the dependence on twist-angle disorder and the open pairing mechanism are the points you raised, and I did not answer them. On B024, I take your worry about the 3D step seriously, but I weigh the original theory pair above the first ARPES observation, as Danielsson argues, so I do not follow you to Hasan in place of Mele. I would accept a citation that says 'topological insulators' broadly enough to cover the 3D case, but I would not add a fourth name.

responses.point: Mehlig reasoned that the pairing mechanism is unsettled and the sample dependence is large in twisted bilayer graphene, and noted that my own slate took Andrei and left out Bistritzer, which seems to reverse the theory priority.
responses.response: That criticism of my allocation was fair. A prize that takes the first-principles prediction of the magic angle seriously could not leave out Bistritzer, and a three-name limit forced a choice I could not make cleanly among four people. That is a sign that the case was not yet ready. I agree with your argument that the Z2 theory should not split Kane from Mele, and I now hold the same trio as you, with the same acknowledgement of the Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang cost. Where I would go further than your citation is on the 2016 prize, which I think the citation text should explicitly distinguish.

responses.point: Kroll holds that the magic-wavelength lattice is a new physical idea, with a two-name credit, many independent laboratories and 1e-18 agreement, and that the pending redefinition of the second depends on rather than defines the achievement.
responses.response: I accept your account of the independent confirmation, which is as strong as for B024, and I would not obstruct B001 on scientific grounds. As a solid-state theorist, I still cannot independently decide whether the lattice clock is distinct from the 2005 comb and the 2012 ion-control prizes, and your answer that the magic-wavelength scheme is a new idea does not settle it for me. I rank B001 as my second alternative. I put B024 first because it adds a new class of quantum matter and an organising concept with a long confirmation record, but I recognise that this is a judgement about the kind of discovery we weigh most.

uncertainties: Whether Kane, Mele and Molenkamp can be defended publicly given the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang (Zhang deceased) and of Hasan, Fu, Moore and Balents.
Whether the 2016 prize on topological phases makes a second topology prize look repetitive, and how explicitly the citation should separate them.
Whether optical lattice clocks carry a distinct physical discovery beyond precision instrumentation, which I cannot judge well from solid-state physics.

Whether the pairing mechanism and disorder dependence in magic-angle graphene will be settled in the next few years, which would change my view on B013 and on the credit among Bistritzer, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Andrei.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. I have no recorded personal or institutional connection to Kane, Mele or Molenkamp, or to the candidates on B013 and B001. My field, first-principles theory of magnetism and electronic structure, is close to topological materials in subject, but I have no joint work or supervision with any credited name. I withdrew my own earlier B013 preference on scientific grounds and not for any personal reason.
